title: Don't Teach Fractions. Not Yet.
author: Dan Murphy
summary: Murphy argues, using the history of mathematics as evidence, that fractions should not be a student's first encounter with rational quantities -- ratios should come first. He points out that Euclid devoted four books of the Elements to ratio and never once wrote a fraction, because for the Greeks (and, he argues, for young children) it is intuitively absurd to split the number one. His pedagogical claim is that ratios express a relationship between two natural numbers, while fractions require introducing an entirely new kind of number, and that skipping straight to fractions forces students to reason about a foreign concept before they've mastered the more natural one. He works through worked examples showing where 'adding ratios' and 'adding fractions' behave identically and where they diverge sharply (combining rates of marble-adding is not the same operation as combining rates of lemonade-making), to show why conflating the two produces classic student errors like 1/3 + 1/2 = 2/5. Murphy then lays out a concrete-pictorial-abstract sequencing that starts students on ratios with real objects, moves to pictorial representations, and only introduces abstract fraction notation once the underlying ratio concept is secure, followed by his proposed order for introducing fraction meanings: fractions as ratios, fractions as parts of a whole, and beyond. The piece is explicitly a curriculum-sequencing argument, not a claim that fractions are inherently too hard for students.
points: Murphy's central claim, grounded in the history of Euclid's Elements, is that ratio is conceptually prior to fraction: fractions require accepting a new kind of number (a part of one), while ratios only require relating counting numbers a child already trusts.

He distinguishes cases where ratio-addition and fraction-addition give the same answer from cases where they diverge sharply (e.g., combining marble ratios vs. combining rate-of-work fractions), arguing that conflating the two operations is the direct source of common student errors like 1/3 + 1/2 = 2/5.

His proposed sequence is concrete-pictorial-abstract: real objects for ratio, then pictures, only then abstract notation -- and abstract fraction symbols like '8:12' or '4/7' should be withheld until after the concrete and pictorial stages are secure.

He introduces the denominator as 'the naming part' and numerator as 'the numbering part' of a fraction (drawing on the Latin roots nomen and numer), reframing a fraction as a count of units whose size is set by the denominator -- explaining why fractions with different denominators can't simply be added.
quotes: Fractions are where math stops making sense for many kids. Not because they're hard. Because we teach them backwards.
Euclid spent four books on ratios. He never wrote a fraction. That's not an oversight but a roadmap we've ignored.

Fractions express parts of unity or one (1). Ratios express a relationship between two natural numbers. Fractions require introducing a new kind of number (rational numbers) into the child’s world. Ratios understood as the relationship between discrete counting numbers does no such thing.

It is important that during the concrete and pictorial stages, we do not yet introduce formal abstract representations of ratios, like “8:12” or “4:3” because this will only get in the way of the understanding.

We cannot add two fractions with different denominators because that would be like trying to add apples and bananas. 3/4 and 5/6 are not 8/10. In the same way, three apples and four bananas are not seven “banan-a-pples.
The concrete-pictorial-abstract approach is exactly why the ordering below matters: ratios first, then parts of a whole, then decimals, then rational numbers. Each step earns the next.
